A tide ledger survives the winter

The harbor town of Wexmoor keeps its tide tables in a ledger older than the lighthouse, and every spring the harbor master copies the year's readings into a fresh volume before the first fishing boats leave.

This year the copying took longer than usual, because the old ledger had been left beside a window during the winter storms and several pages had swollen and stuck together along their lower edges.

A bookbinder from the next valley spent three afternoons easing the pages apart with a thin bone folder, a pot of warm water and a great deal of patience, and only two entries were lost entirely.

Those two entries recorded the lowest tides of a February week, and the harbor master reconstructed them from the logbooks of the ferry, which crosses the bay twice a day and notes the depth at the pier.

The ferry captain was pleased to help, though she pointed out that her logbooks round every depth to the nearest half fathom, so the reconstructed figures are less precise than the ones around them.

The new ledger marks both entries with a small circle in the margin and a note explaining where the numbers came from, which the harbor master says is the only honest way to keep a record like this.

Visitors who want to see the old ledger can ask at the harbor office on weekday mornings, where it now rests in a dry cabinet with a glass front and a small card describing the winter it nearly did not survive.

The bookbinder has offered to rebind the old volume in the autumn, once the pages have dried completely, and the town council will decide in its September meeting whether to pay for new boards and thread.
